items.title: Only the tune changes
items.caption: The words and their order stay the same. An English yes or no question lifts the voice at the end; a Samoan one usually falls and stays low over the last two or three syllables.

states.label: Statement
states.note: A statement. The book never marks its tune.

states.label: Samoan question
states.note: The same three words. The voice falls and stays low at the end, which is what the arrow ↘ marks in this book.

states.label: English question
states.note: English runs the other way: its yes or no question lifts the voice at the end.

items.title: From sleeping to putting to sleep
items.caption: Step through it: the verb, the verb with *faʻa-* in front, then the built word at work in a sentence. The highlight marks what each step adds to the one before.

states.label: The verb
states.note: *Moe* takes no doer of its own: it names something one person does with nobody else in the sentence.

states.label: Add *faʻa-*
states.note: *Faʻa-* goes on the front and never changes its own shape, and the two are written together as one word. The built word means to make somebody do what *moe* names.

states.label: In a sentence
states.sm: Sā faʻamoe e le teine le pepe.
states.en: The girl put the baby to sleep.
states.note: Now the sentence holds two people: the doer, *le teine*, carrying the agent marker *e*, and the one it was done to, *le pepe*, standing bare after the verb.
